The defeat meant the Reds crashed out of the eight-team regional tournament, taking place in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, with a game of the group stage remaining.

Two years later, the capital city came under the control of the Houthis, an Iran-backed militant group, provoking a Saudi-led intervention and years of fighting. In early September, the Houthis swept down the Red Sea coast in its first major military advance in five years and have been targeting Riyadh and other places in Saudi Arabia with missile strikes.

At the time, the national team had been training in the southern port city of Aden, home of the presidential leadership council, Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed, governing body. “The situation in Aden was OK. We tried our best and had a training camp with local players and then we joined up with the rest of the squad in Jeddah,” Ould Ali says.

“The situation is a political situation and it is not stable. In football we have to be careful. We have a lot of attention on outside factors, but we always try to focus on the football and do better. “The league stopped for a long time and restarted this year and they finished the first half of the season,” Ould Ali says. “It is very important. The players need to play, need to keep fit and show their talent.

“The people support us. It is a religion in Yemen. Everyone likes football and the national team and follows their star players. The Yemeni people are the same as anyone else.”

Most of the players are based at home and before the 27th edition of the Gulf Cup, Yemen was the only one of the eight never to have won the tournament and have never got out of the group.

It is hard for the players to keep fully focused on football while in Saudi Arabia. “They worry about what is going on in the country and they hope their families are OK,” the coach said. “This is normal, but they are professional and I ask them to try to focus on the games.
